questions.q: Why does this course treat the Well-Architected Framework's five pillars as 'shared vocabulary' rather than as a checklist?
options: The pillars are meant to replace the IaC and container tooling from earlier courses
The real value is giving everyone in a design review the same words to point at the same kinds of problems, not producing a one-time score
A checklist score is legally required for cloud compliance audits
Vendors update the pillar list too often for a checklist to stay accurate
questions.explain: The framework's value is as a common language — naming a specific pillar and failure mode is far more actionable in a review than vague, un-anchored concern.

questions.q: Which five pillars appear in both Microsoft's Azure Well-Architected Framework and AWS's Well-Architected Framework?
options: Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence, Performance Efficiency
Scalability, Portability, Compliance, Latency, Throughput
Governance, Automation, Observability, Resilience, Agility
Availability, Durability, Elasticity, Consistency, Partition Tolerance
questions.explain: Both vendors converged on the same five pillars, under nearly identical names, even though the order they're published in differs slightly between the two frameworks.

questions.q: What do the Azure WAF Review and the AWS Well-Architected Tool have in common?
options: They are paid, consulting-only services with no public access
They only evaluate security, not the other four pillars
They are free, vendor-hosted, guided self-assessments a team runs against a real workload, scored pillar by pillar
They automatically rewrite Terraform code to fix any pillar violations they find
questions.explain: Both are free, guided self-assessment tools published by their respective vendors, used to score a real workload against each of the five pillars.

questions.q: A reviewer says a design 'feels kind of risky.' According to this lesson, what's the problem with that framing compared to naming a specific pillar and failure mode?
options: Nothing — vague framing and pillar-specific framing are equally actionable
It's too technical for a design review audience
It only applies to AWS workloads, not Azure ones
It isn't actionable — it doesn't point to a specific kind of problem or invite a specific kind of fix the way naming the pillar does
questions.explain: Pillar-anchored language ('this introduces a single point of failure in the reliability pillar') is specific and actionable; 'feels risky' gives the room nothing concrete to respond to.

questions.q: Does the order in which Azure and AWS publish their five pillars imply that one pillar matters more than another?
options: Yes — the first pillar listed is always the highest priority for that vendor
No — publication order differs slightly between the two vendors and does not imply priority; a system can fail on any pillar
Yes, but only for Azure's framework, not AWS's
The pillars are not actually ordered at all in either framework
questions.explain: The two vendors list the same five pillars in slightly different orders, and neither order is a priority ranking — a workload can fail on cost just as easily as on reliability.
